reference.source: Clinical genetics and neurodevelopmental textbooks with peer-reviewed reviews
clinicalPearls: Neurodevelopmental disorder caused by a recurrent interstitial deletion of chromosome 17p11.2 encompassing RAI1, or by a pathogenic variant within RAI1 itself

Cardinal feature is a severely disrupted circadian sleep-wake rhythm with an inverted melatonin cycle (melatonin secreted during the day rather than at night), causing daytime sleepiness and marked night-time waking
Characteristic behavioural phenotype includes self-injurious behaviours (notably nail-yanking and inserting objects into body orifices) and self-hugging or hand-squeezing stereotypies
Intellectual disability, developmental delay, and expressive speech difficulties are typical, alongside a generally sociable but impulsive temperament
Recognisable dysmorphic features include a broad, square face, brachycephaly, midface hypoplasia, and a tented upper lip, evolving with age
Associated medical issues include hearing loss, ophthalmological problems, scoliosis, and features that may mimic other neurodevelopmental syndromes
Management of the sleep disturbance addresses the abnormal melatonin rhythm and sleep hygiene, and behavioural and developmental support is central to care
Diagnosis is established by chromosomal microarray to detect the 17p11.2 deletion, or by RAI1 sequencing when a deletion is not found
reference.pathophysiology: Smith-Magenis syndrome results from haploinsufficiency of RAI1 (retinoic acid-induced 1), whether through the common 17p11.2 microdeletion or a point variant within the gene. RAI1 is a transcriptional regulator with widespread roles in neurodevelopment and, importantly, in the control of circadian gene expression. Reduced RAI1 dosage disrupts the molecular circadian clock, producing the hallmark inversion of the melatonin secretion rhythm and the resulting sleep-wake disturbance, while its broader transcriptional effects account for the cognitive, behavioural, craniofacial, and multisystem features of the syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Down syndrome and other chromosomal microdeletion/duplication syndromes
Autism spectrum disorder with sleep disturbance
Other syndromic intellectual disability with self-injurious behaviour
additionalInvestigations: Chromosomal microarray to detect the 17p11.2 deletion
RAI1 sequencing when microarray is normal but the phenotype is suggestive
Assessment of the circadian rhythm and melatonin profile where sleep disturbance is prominent
Audiological and ophthalmological evaluation for associated sensory deficits
Skeletal assessment for scoliosis and developmental/behavioural evaluation
redFlags: Severe self-injurious behaviour causing significant tissue damage
Profound sleep deprivation affecting safety and daytime functioning
New or worsening scoliosis with respiratory or neurological compromise
Acute behavioural crisis posing risk to the patient or others
reference.prognosis: Smith-Magenis syndrome is a lifelong condition; intellectual disability and behavioural and sleep difficulties persist, but life expectancy is generally not markedly reduced and structured behavioural, sleep, and developmental interventions can meaningfully improve quality of life.
pitfalls: Attributing the sleep disturbance to primary behavioural insomnia and missing the underlying inverted melatonin rhythm
Overlooking the diagnosis in a child labelled with non-syndromic autism or intellectual disability
Failing to recognise the characteristic self-injurious and self-hugging behaviours as diagnostic clues
Not arranging chromosomal microarray, or stopping at a normal microarray without considering RAI1 sequencing
references: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
management: Target the inverted circadian rhythm with evening melatonin and daytime beta-adrenergic blockade using acebutolol to suppress aberrant daytime melatonin, alongside structured sleep hygiene.
Behavioural management of self-injurious and stereotypic behaviours with structured behavioural intervention and, where needed, psychotropic agents.
Early developmental support with speech and language therapy, occupational therapy and individualised education for intellectual disability.
Surveillance for associated problems including hearing loss, ophthalmological disease, scoliosis, and thyroid, lipid and renal abnormalities.
Coordinate care across clinical genetics, developmental paediatrics or neurology, psychiatry and relevant sensory specialists.
Family and educational support with consistent routines and behavioural strategies to improve quality of life.
Genetic counselling explaining the usually de novo chromosome 17p11.2 deletion or RAI1 variant and the correspondingly low recurrence risk.
